title: Jormungand
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: Koko Hekmatyar, a young arms dealer for the shipping giant HCLI, travels the world selling weapons with a squad of ex-soldier bodyguards. Her newest guard is Jonah, a child soldier who lost his family to war and hates arms dealers. Over eleven volumes Koko reveals a plan, called Jormungand, to force world peace at an enormous human cost.
life_message: Loyalty to the people beside you matters most in a world run by violence, while the price of peace remains an open question.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Crew answer threats personally and with guns rather than through courts.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Koko works outside national law, evading local and international authorities (Wikipedia).

Civic vs kin.evidence: The squad functions as a chosen family; loyalty to crew over states.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Koko commands her team; respect earned by competence.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Purely secular calculation of costs and benefits drives the plot.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Security, survival and practical skill dominate; little room for self-expression.

folkways.japan: The multinational setting shows few specifically Japanese norms; the crew's loyalty to its leader echoes group-harmony ideals common in Japanese storytelling.

delivery.evidence: ANN: ideas on war and peace come through dialogue debates between Koko and Jonah, raised but left half-finished.

personified.ideology: peace imposed by force; sacrifice some for many

delivery.note: Koko's and Jonah's opposing views are argued in conversation, and the ending leaves the question unresolved.

winners_losers: Koko appears poised to carry out her plan and Jonah returns after a time skip, so neither view clearly wins; sympathy rests with Jonah's doubts and the crew's loyalty.
